lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: You know that old man—the extremely old one, I mean—Eucrates, the rich fellow with no children and about fifty thousand men hunting his estate?

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Yes. The man from Sicyon. What about him?

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Let him live, Hermes. He has had ninety years already; measure him out another ninety on top of that. More, if it can be arranged. But his flatterers—young Charinus, Damon, and the rest—drag them down here one after another. All of them.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: That may look a little odd.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Not odd. Perfectly fair. What exactly have they suffered, that they should pray for the man to die? What claim have they on his money, when they are no kin of his? And the filthiest part is this: while praying for just that, they still dance attendance on him in public. When he is ill, everyone can see what they are thinking; still they promise sacrifices if he recovers. Their flattery has more colours than a bad cloak. So let him be immortal, for all I care. Let them go first, with their mouths open for nothing.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: They will look ridiculous. Serves them; they are scoundrels. And the old man plays them along beautifully—keeps them hopeful. He looks permanently dead, and is somehow much healthier than the young men. They have already divided the inheritance among themselves and are fattening on a blessed life entirely in their own heads.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Good. Let him slip off old age like Iolaus and turn young again. As for them, let them be pulled out from the middle of their expectations, leave behind the fortune they dreamed of, and come here at once—bad men dying badly.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Leave it to me, Pluto. I’ll go fetch them for you now, one by one. There are seven of them, I think.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Drag them down. And he can send each one off in his place, getting back his first youth every time.
